theory.intro: Slicing a solid gives a **cross-section**. A **prism** is a solid whose cross-section stays exactly the same all the way through: every slice parallel to the base is identical to the base.
facts: A **cross-section** is the shape formed when a solid is "sliced".
A solid has a **uniform cross-section** when every slice parallel to the base is **identical** to the base — the same shape **and** the same size.
The **base** of a prism is its pair of identical, parallel end faces. It is not always the face the solid is resting on.
The uniform cross-section of a prism is a **polygon**, a shape with straight sides. A cylinder has a uniform cross-section, but it is a circle, so a cylinder is **not** a prism.
A pyramid or a cone has slices that shrink towards the apex, so it has no uniform cross-section.
steps: Find the pair of identical, parallel end faces and take one of them as the base.
Imagine slicing the solid parallel to the base.
Check whether every slice is identical to the base — the same shape and the same size.

foundation.solution_text:
The base of this prism has six straight sides.
Every slice parallel to the base is identical to the base, so the cross-section is a hexagon.

The base of this prism has three straight sides.
Every slice parallel to the base is identical to the base, so the cross-section is a triangle.

The base of a cylinder is a circle, and the cylinder is the same width all the way up.
Every slice parallel to the base is identical to the base, so the cross-section is a circle.

Slice the solid parallel to the base and every slice is the same rectangle, the same shape and the same size.
So the solid has a uniform cross-section, and because a rectangle is a polygon the solid is a prism.

Each slice parallel to the base is a square, but the squares get smaller the closer the slice is to the top point.
The slices are not identical, so the solid does not have a uniform cross-section.

Each slice parallel to the base is a circle, but the circles shrink towards the point at the top.
The slices are not identical, so the solid does not have a uniform cross-section.

The base of a prism is its pair of identical, parallel end faces.
The two triangular faces at the ends are identical and parallel, and the rectangular faces are not.
So a triangular end face is the base, even though the prism is resting on a rectangle.

development.solution_text:
The base of this prism is a four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides.
Every slice parallel to the base is identical to the base, so the cross-section is a trapezium.

This slice is not parallel to the base, so it is not the circle you get from a horizontal slice.
It cuts the base along a straight line and rises to the single point at the top, giving three straight edges.
The cross-section is a triangle.

The slice cuts through both sloping faces and through both end faces.
It has four straight sides meeting at right angles, so the cross-section is a rectangle.

The uniform cross-section of a prism matches its base, and the base is the pair of identical, parallel end faces.
Here those end faces are the six-sided faces at each end, not the rectangle the prism is resting on.
The uniform cross-section is a hexagon.

The two trapezium-shaped end faces are identical and parallel, so a trapezium face is the base.
The height of a prism is the perpendicular distance between the two bases.
So the height is measured along the length of the solid, from one trapezium face to the other.

The slices all have the same shape, but the higher the slice the smaller the rectangle.
A uniform cross-section needs every slice to be identical, the same shape **and** the same size.
So the solid does not have a uniform cross-section.

mastery.solution_text:
A uniform cross-section is tested with slices taken parallel to the **base**, and the base of this prism is a trapezium-shaped end face.
Slices parallel to the ground are not parallel to those end faces, so they say nothing about whether the solid is a prism.
Slices taken parallel to a trapezium end face are all the same trapezium, the same shape and the same size.
Every slice parallel to the base is identical, so the solid is a prism.

Every slice parallel to the base is a circle, so the student is right that the slices all have the same **shape**.
But the circles get smaller the closer the slice is to the point at the top, so the slices are not the same **size**.
A uniform cross-section needs the slices to be identical, so the cone does not have one.

Every slice of solid $A$ parallel to its base is the same circle, and every slice of solid $B$ parallel to its base is the same pentagon, so both solids do have a uniform cross-section.
The uniform cross-section of a prism must also be a polygon, a shape with straight sides.
A circle has no straight sides but a pentagon has five, so solid $B$ is the prism.
